lessons.title: Farsi Script and Direction
lessons.explanation: Farsi (Persian) uses a modified Arabic script written right-to-left. It has 32 letters. Four letters not in Arabic: پ (p), چ (ch), ژ (zh), گ (g). Vowels are usually not written in everyday text — readers infer them from context.
examples: پ (pe) — like English P
چ (che) — like English CH
ژ (zhe) — like French J in 'jour'
گ (gaf) — like English G
lessons.tip: Start by learning the four uniquely Persian letters and the shape groups of the Arabic letters.

quiz.question: Which letter exists in Farsi but NOT in Arabic?
In which direction is Farsi written?

lessons.title: Pronouns — ضمایر
lessons.explanation: Farsi personal pronouns: من (man) = I, تو (to) = you (informal), او/وی (u/vey) = he/she/it, ما (mā) = we, شما (shomā) = you (formal/plural), آن‌ها/ایشان (ān-hā/ishān) = they. Note: Farsi has NO gender distinction in third person.
examples: من دانش‌آموز هستم. (Man dānesh-āmuz hastam.) — I am a student.
تو دوست من هستی. (To dust-e man hasti.) — You are my friend.
او معلم است. (U mo'allem ast.) — He/She is a teacher.
ما ایرانی هستیم. (Mā Irāni hastim.) — We are Iranian.
lessons.tip: A great feature of Farsi: او (u) means both he AND she — no need to track gender in third person!

quiz.question: How do you say 'I' in Farsi?
Does Farsi distinguish he/she with different pronouns?
options: no, او is used for both

lessons.title: The Verb 'To Be' — بودن
lessons.explanation: Present tense of بودن (budan — to be): هستم (hastam = I am), هستی (hasti = you are), است/هست (ast/hast = he/she is), هستیم (hastim = we are), هستید (hastid = you pl. are), هستند (hastand = they are). In informal speech, است contracts to ـه (-e) or ـَست (-ast).
examples: من خوب هستم. (Man khub hastam.) — I am good/fine.
او معلم است. (U mo'allem ast.) — He/She is a teacher.
ما خوشحال هستیم. (Mā khoshhāl hastim.) — We are happy.
آنها ایرانی هستند. (Ān-hā Irāni hastand.) — They are Iranian.
lessons.tip: In informal speech, است often becomes just ـَه (-e): معلمه = (is a) teacher.

lessons.title: SOV Order and Ezafe
lessons.explanation: Farsi is SOV (Subject-Object-Verb). The verb goes LAST. The Ezafe construction (ِـ) links a noun to what modifies it: noun + ِـ + modifier. Example: کتاب‌ِ من (my book, literally 'book of me'). Adjectives also use Ezafe: کتاب‌ِ آبی (the blue book).
examples: من کتاب می‌خوانم. (Man ketāb mi-khānam.) — I (am) reading a book.
خانه‌ی من بزرگ است. (My house is big.) — Ezafe possessive
کتاب آبی (the blue book) — adjective after noun via Ezafe
دوست خوب (good friend) — Ezafe linking noun and adjective
lessons.tip: Ezafe is written as a short vowel ِـ after the noun. In everyday writing, it's often omitted and readers infer it.

quiz.question: What does the Ezafe construction do in Farsi?
options: links a noun to its modifier

lessons.title: Present Tense — می‌ + Verb Stem
lessons.explanation: Farsi present/continuous tense uses the prefix می‌ (mi-) + present stem + personal ending. Present stem of رفتن (to go) is رو (ro). Personal endings: -م, -ی, -د, -یم, -ید, -ند.
examples: می‌روم (mi-ravam) — I go/am going
می‌روی (mi-ravi) — you go
می‌رود (mi-ravad) — he/she goes
می‌خوانیم (mi-khānim) — we read
می‌خورند (mi-khorand) — they eat
lessons.tip: می‌ is like the English '-ing' marker — it signals an ongoing or habitual action in the present.

quiz.question: What prefix marks the present tense in Farsi?

lessons.title: Past Tense — Past Stem + Personal Endings
lessons.explanation: Farsi past tense uses the past stem + personal endings: -م, -ی, — (3rd sg. = zero suffix), -یم, -ید, -ند. The past stem is found by removing -ن from the infinitive. رفتن → رفت (raft) + endings: رفتم, رفتی, رفت, رفتیم, رفتید, رفتند.
examples: رفتم (raftam) — I went
دیدی (didi) — you saw
خورد (khord) — he/she ate
گفتیم (goftim) — we said
آمدند (āmadand) — they came
lessons.tip: The 3rd person singular past has NO ending — the bare past stem IS the 3rd person past: رفت = he/she went.

quiz.question: What is the past stem of رفتن (to go)?

lessons.title: Subjunctive and Indirect Speech
lessons.explanation: The Farsi subjunctive uses the prefix بـ (be-) + present stem + personal endings. Used after verbs of wanting, wishing, commanding, and after که (that) with certain expressions.
examples: می‌خواهم بروم. (I want to go.) — subjunctive
بگذار بیاید. (Let him/her come.) — subjunctive
امیدوارم که بیایی. (I hope that you come.) — subjunctive
ممکن است برود. (He/she may go.) — subjunctive
lessons.tip: The Farsi subjunctive looks like بـ + present stem, while the indicative uses می‌ + present stem. Swap می‌ for بـ.

quiz.question: What prefix marks the Farsi subjunctive?
